name: Alexander technique

image.caption: Learning Alexander Technique with Graham Fandrei (28692247726)

lead: The Alexander technique teaches people to notice and change habitual movement and posture patterns, typically through private lessons with a trained teacher. Users take it to sit, stand and walk more upright, for a taller, more balanced presence. It was developed by the actor Frederick Matthias Alexander from the 1890s.

Teachers use verbal cues and light hands-on guidance during everyday activities, aiming to reduce unnecessary muscle tension and change habitual patterns. Randomised trials have tested it for chronic back and neck pain and Parkinson's disease; the largest, the ATEAM trial in England, found lessons reduced back-pain-related disability compared with usual care. Appearance outcomes have not been studied.

paras: People attend individual lessons, usually 30 to 60 minutes, and practise the cues in daily activities. Changes build over a series of lessons and are meant to carry over into how you sit, stand and walk.

Few trials report safety data. Some health bodies say advocates' claims go beyond the evidence, and at least one insurer classes it as experimental. Teaching is not statutorily regulated in the UK, so teacher training varies.

angle.text: Alexander technique lessons retrain movement habits, so sitting and standing posture improves and you carry yourself taller and more upright. Trials have studied it for back and neck pain.

lead: The Alexander technique is a method of movement and posture re-education named after Frederick Matthias Alexander (1869-1955), an actor who began developing it in the 1890s to deal with voice loss during performance [1][2]. It is taught in individual lessons, usually 30 to 60 minutes, using verbal cues and gentle touch during activities such as sitting, standing and walking [1].

People interested in their appearance turn to it as a way to change how they carry themselves: a head balanced over the spine, less slouching and a more open chest and neck line change the silhouette seen in profile and from the front, and also how tall and relaxed a person looks. Students are taught to notice habitual tension and to release it while moving, often practising in front of a mirror [1].

Randomised trials have tested it mainly for chronic or recurrent low back pain, chronic neck pain and Parkinson's disease [3][4][5]. The largest, the ATEAM trial in England, found that lessons reduced back-pain-related disability compared with usual care [3]. A systematic review of controlled trials in musicians also examined posture and body use as outcomes [6].
No published study has tested whether the technique changes physical appearance, facial balance or attractiveness.

paras: Frederick Matthias Alexander was born on 20 January 1869 near Wynyard, Tasmania, the eldest of ten children of a blacksmith, and moved to Melbourne in 1889 to pursue acting and elocution.[2] Recurring hoarseness and breathing problems hampered his acting career; according to his biography on Wikipedia, he studied his own speaking habits with mirrors and concluded that inhibiting wrong movements, rather than forcing correct ones, was the key, although later scholars note the ideas developed gradually.[2][1] The article on the technique dates one stage of this thinking to a recital tour of New Zealand in 1895 and says it was less systematic and slower than often portrayed.[1]

He worked as a reciter and voice teacher, opening a practice in Melbourne in 1896 and moving to Sydney in 1900. In 1902 a surgeon encouraged him to focus on medical referrals and to move to London, where he arrived in June 1904.[2] There he built a practice supported by an ear, nose and throat surgeon and prominent actors, and published the books Man's Supreme Inheritance (1910) and Conscious Control (1912).[2]

The technique was not originally conceived as therapy but has since become a form of complementary medicine.[1] The philosopher John Dewey, who became a pupil in the United States in 1916, said that headaches, neck pain, blurred vision and stress symptoms largely improved while he applied Alexander's advice on posture, and in 1923 wrote the introduction to Constructive Conscious Control of the Individual.[1][2] Fritz Perls, founder of Gestalt therapy, credited Alexander as an inspiration.[1] Other pupils and admirers named in his biography include Aldous Huxley, George Bernard Shaw, Charles Sherrington and Moshe Feldenkrais, and Nikolaas Tinbergen praised the technique in his 1973 Nobel lecture.[2]

Alexander returned to London in 1924, began formal teacher training in 1931, and published The Use of the Self (1932) and The Universal Constant in Living (1941); training was suspended in 1940 during the war and resumed after 1943.[2] As of 1995 the technique was on the curriculum of prominent Western performing arts institutions, where it is used to improve voice and posture.[1] The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health classifies it as a psychological and physical complementary approach used alongside mainstream medicine.[1]

Wikipedia's biography records that Ernst Jokl, a South African government physical education director, described the technique as quackery in a 1944 article, and Alexander sued for libel.[2] Proceedings ran in London and Johannesburg; Alexander suffered strokes in late 1947 but stayed involved, and in March 1948 the Johannesburg court awarded him 1,000 pounds plus costs, with the defendants' appeal failing a year later.[2] Alexander died in London on 10 October 1955, aged 86, and his London practice passed to his assistant Patrick Macdonald.[2]

Lessons typically involve chair work, walking, and table work, sometimes with a mirror, and students are regarded as learners rather than patients [1][7]. A 2014 paper grouped it with other movement-based contemplative practices [7]. In the UK professional bodies offer voluntary membership and multi-year training [1].

The professional teaching tradition describes the method as intentional inhibition of unwanted habitual behaviours and re-education of movement patterns, according to a systematic review that studied it in musicians [6]. Wikipedia notes that students include performers, computer workers and people in frequent pain, and that a 2014 review described the approach as educational, with students rather than patients [1].

In the UK there is no statutory regulation of teachers; professional organisations offer voluntary membership and multi-year training, and a 2015 UK survey cited by Wikipedia found most affiliated practitioners were university-educated and self-employed.[1] Wikipedia also notes that table work involves hands-on guidance, while chair work, often in front of a mirror, covers standing, sitting and walking.[1]

The visual changes people look for are those of carriage: a head that sits balanced over the spine rather than pushed forward, shoulders that are not rounded, and a neck that lengthens in profile. Teachers describe the method as releasing habitual tension rather than holding a corrected position, and students often work in front of a mirror during chair work.[1] Those who care about how they stand and sit therefore use lessons as a way to retrain everyday habits, with the lessons' stated aim being movement and function and the visible effect on posture being the reason people in appearance communities mention it.[1][8]

In appearance communities the technique is mentioned alongside corrective exercise and mobility work as a way to retrain posture. A T Nation forum user once recommended it to another member as a relaxation and alignment approach that helps with neck problems [8]. Strength trainees also discuss technique cues such as staying upright under load, which overlap in spirit with posture awareness [9].

In the musicians review, posture and body use were among the measured outcomes, and the authors assessed 12 studies (5 randomised and 5 non-randomised controlled trials, plus 2 mixed-methods studies) [6]. The ATEAM trial and the neck-pain trial measured pain and disability rather than appearance [3][4].

The ATEAM randomised trial enrolled 579 patients with chronic or recurrent back pain in 64 English general practices, randomised to normal care, massage, six Alexander lessons or 24 lessons, with half of each group also given an exercise prescription. At one year, exercise and Alexander lessons, but not massage, remained effective against the control Roland disability score of 8.1: the reductions were 1.40 points after six lessons and 3.4 after 24 lessons, and exercise after six lessons reached about 72 percent of the effect of 24 lessons alone. Days in pain over four weeks fell by 18 after 24 lessons versus a control median of 21, and the authors reported no significant harms.[3] An accompanying economic evaluation was published.[10]

A 2015 three-group trial in UK primary care enrolled 517 people with neck pain lasting at least three months (median six years) and compared 20 one-to-one Alexander lessons or 12 acupuncture sessions, plus usual care, with usual care alone. At 12 months, Northwick Park neck-pain scores were reduced by about 3.8 percentage points more with Alexander lessons (p = 0.010) and 3.9 with acupuncture (p = 0.009) than with usual care alone; the authors noted that practitioners came from the two main UK professional associations and that self-efficacy may partly explain sustained benefits.[4]

A 2002 randomised trial in 93 people with idiopathic Parkinson's disease compared 24 Alexander lessons, 24 massage sessions and no additional intervention; the lesson group improved on the disability scale compared with the no-intervention group both after treatment and at six months, and was less depressed after treatment.[5] A 2022 randomised trial in 80 patients with chronic low back pain in Kashan, Iran, found lower pain scores in the group given three 60-minute sessions a week for 12 weeks than in the control group.[11] A case report described improved automatic postural coordination after lessons in one person with low back pain.[12]

A 2014 systematic review of controlled trials in musicians identified 237 citations and included 12 studies (5 randomised trials, 5 non-randomised controlled trials and 2 mixed-methods studies). It reported that performance anxiety was reduced in 2 of 2 randomised trials and 2 of 2 controlled trials, and that effects on music performance, respiratory function and posture were inconclusive.[6] A 2012 Cochrane review assessed the technique for chronic asthma.[13]

Wikipedia summarises that the NHS says some evidence exists for chronic back or neck pain and possible benefit for Parkinson's disease, while NICE recommends that people with Parkinson's with balance or motor problems consider it alongside physiotherapy; it records that the NHS found no good evidence for asthma, headaches, osteoarthritis, sleep difficulties or stress, and that a 2015 review found safety reporting in trials lacking.[1] No studies found examining the technique's effect on facial appearance, symmetry or attractiveness.

According to Wikipedia, the UK NHS and NICE cite evidence that it may help long-term back and neck pain, while the NHS notes that advocates' claims go beyond the evidence. In 2017 the Australian government excluded it from private health insurance rebates, and in 2021 the insurer Aetna classed it as experimental and investigational [1].

Wikipedia also records that a 2015 Australian government review found that it may improve short-term pain and disability in low back pain, that longer-term effects were uncertain, and that safety was rarely reported in trials [1].
